stem: A company is moving an application to Amazon EC2 instances in two Availability Zones. The instances must read and write the same set of files at the same time. The instances run Linux and access the files over NFS. The company wants to move the files from its data center to AWS without changing the application. Which storage solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: The instances run Linux and access the files over NFS

options.text: Create an Amazon EFS file system with a mount target in each Availability Zone, and mount the file system on every instance.
options.why: The Linux instances keep their NFS mounts, because EFS uses [NFS v4](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-nfs-v4-protocol) and serves instances in several zones [concurrently from multiple NFS clients](../facts/efs.md#efs-concurrent-access-multiple-clients-multiple-azs).

options.text: Create an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ file system that is joined to Active Directory, and map its share on every instance.
options.why: It serves files over [the SMB protocol](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-faq-windows-smb-protocol) and needs an Active Directory domain, which the Linux NFS clients do not use.
options.misconception: picks the Windows SMB file system for Linux clients that use NFS

options.text: Install file server software on a new EC2 instance with a large Amazon EBS volume, and share the files from it with every instance.
options.why: It can work, but the company runs and patches the file server itself, while EFS is [serverless, fully elastic file storage](../facts/efs.md#efs-serverless-elastic-no-provisioning).

options.text: Create one Amazon EBS io2 volume with Multi-Attach turned on, and attach the volume to every instance in both Availability Zones.
options.why: Multi-Attach attaches one io2 volume to instances [in the same Availability Zone](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-same-az), so the instances in the second zone cannot attach it.

explanation: Linux clients that share files over NFS fit Amazon EFS. A Regional file system stores data across [multiple geographically separated Availability Zones](../facts/efs.md#efs-regional-recommended-type), and each zone gets a mount target, so both zones read and write the same files. AWS runs the storage, so the company has no file server to patch.
takeaway: Linux instances that share files over NFS across zones: Amazon EFS.
twin: If the stem said "The instances run Windows Server, and users reach the files through SMB shares with permissions from the company's Active Directory" instead: FSx for Windows File Server, because EFS on Windows instances [is not supported](../facts/efs.md#efs-windows-ec2-not-supported).
say: Linux and NFS across zones means EFS: a managed shared file system with a mount target in each zone.

stem: A company stores about 100 GiB of application data on an Amazon EFS Regional file system that uses Bursting throughput. The file system has used all of its burst credits, and the application slows down. The throughput is spiky and unpredictable: the application is idle most of the day, then drives short peaks. The company must restore the performance of the application. Which change will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

options.text: Switch the file system to Elastic throughput, so that throughput scales up and down with the reads and writes of the application.
options.why: Elastic fits [spiky or unpredictable workloads](../facts/efs.md#efs-elastic-best-for-spiky-low-average-to-peak), and you [pay only for the amount of metadata](../facts/efs.md#efs-elastic-scales-automatically-no-provisioning-pay-per-use) and data that the application reads and writes.

options.text: Switch the file system to Provisioned throughput, and set the provisioned level to the throughput that the application needs at its peak.
options.why: It works, but you are [charged for the amount of throughput enabled](../facts/efs.md#efs-provisioned-billed-for-throughput-enabled) all day, although the application is idle most of the time.

options.text: Keep Bursting throughput, and store extra unused data in the file system to raise the baseline throughput that the file system earns.
options.why: Bursting gives [throughput that scales with the amount of storage](../facts/efs.md#efs-bursting-scales-with-storage-size-recommended-for), so the company pays to store data that nobody reads.

options.text: Create a new file system that uses the Max I/O performance mode, and copy the application data to the new file system.
options.why: Max I/O changes the performance mode, not the throughput mode, and AWS recommends [always using General Purpose performance mode](../facts/efs.md#efs-general-purpose-always-recommended-max-io-higher-latency).

explanation: The file system ran out of burst credits, and its load is spiky and unpredictable. Elastic throughput [scales automatically](../facts/efs.md#efs-elastic-scales-automatically-no-provisioning-pay-per-use), so the short peaks get the throughput that they need. The company pays for the reads and writes, not for a level that stays unused through the idle hours.
takeaway: Spiky or unpredictable EFS throughput: Elastic throughput, which charges for what the application uses.
twin: If the stem said "The application drives a steady-state, predictable throughput close to its peak all day" instead: Provisioned throughput, because it fits [predictable and high levels of sustained throughput requirements](../facts/efs.md#efs-pricing-provisioned-throughput-predictable-sustained).
say: Spiky and hard to forecast means Elastic throughput: it scales with the load, and you pay for what you use.

stem: A company runs a Linux application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The instances share a set of files through an Amazon EFS file system. The files are development build artifacts that the team can re-create, and a loss of access during an Availability Zone outage is acceptable. The company plans to create a new file system for these files. Which file system configuration will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: development build artifacts that the team can re-create
a loss of access during an Availability Zone outage is acceptable

options.text: Create an EFS One Zone file system in one Availability Zone, and keep the automatic backups of the new file system turned on.
options.why: One Zone suits [development, build, and staging environments](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-one-zone-use-cases), and the stem accepts a loss of access during a zone outage.

options.text: Create an EFS Regional file system that stores data across Availability Zones, and create a mount target in each zone.
options.why: It works, but it pays for availability that the stem does not need, because One Zone fits applications that [do not require the Multi-AZ availability and durability](../facts/efs.md#efs-pricing-one-zone-for-no-multi-az-need).

options.text: Create an EFS Regional file system, and configure EFS Replication to a destination file system in a second AWS Region.
options.why: It works, but it adds a second file system in a [Region or Availability Zone (AZ) of your choice](../facts/efs.md#efs-replication-destination-faq-region-or-az-of-choice) for files that the team can re-create.
options.misconception: adds a second Region for files that the team can re-create

options.text: Create two EFS One Zone file systems in two Availability Zones, and keep them in sync with a scheduled AWS DataSync task.
options.why: Two file systems and a sync task cost more than one One Zone file system, and the stem accepts a loss of access during a zone outage.
options.misconception: keeps two copies in sync instead of choosing the file system type that fits

explanation: The team can re-create the files, and the stem accepts a loss of access during a zone outage. One Zone file systems [store data redundantly within a single AZ](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-one-zone-single-az), and AWS names them for [development, build, and staging environments](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-one-zone-use-cases). One file system in one zone is the cheapest configuration that meets the requirements.
takeaway: Re-creatable development files and an accepted zone outage: EFS One Zone.
twin: If the stem said "The files are production reports, and the file system must be highly available if one Availability Zone fails" instead: a Regional file system, because it gives [continuous availability to the data](../facts/efs.md#efs-regional-multi-az-continuous-availability).

stem: A company runs a serverless document-processing application. Many AWS Lambda functions run at the same time, and all of them must read and update the same set of files with standard file operations. The files must persist between invocations and must be visible to every function. The functions already connect to a VPC in one AWS Region. Which storage solution meets these requirements?
keywords: the same set of files with standard file operations

options.text: Write the files to the /tmp directory of each function, and read the files back from /tmp in later invocations.
options.why: /tmp is [temporary and unique to each execution environment](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-tmp-unique-per-environment), so other functions do not see the files, and the files do not persist.

options.text: Create an Amazon EBS gp3 volume, and attach the volume to each function when the function starts to process a request.
options.why: Block storage is [attached to single Amazon EC2 instances or containers](../facts/efs.md#efs-decision-guide-block-row-single-instance), so it is not a file system that many functions share.
options.misconception: believes that a function can attach a block volume as an instance does

options.text: Create an Amazon EFS file system with mount targets in the VPC, and configure each function to mount the file system.
options.why: A function can [mount an Amazon Elastic File System](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-efs-shared-mount-in-vpc) to a local directory and [access and modify shared resources safely](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-efs-shared-mount-in-vpc) at high concurrency.

options.text: Store the files as objects in an Amazon S3 bucket, and read and write the objects with the S3 API from each function.
options.why: S3 is an [object storage service](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-use-case-file-vs-block-vs-object), so the code uses API calls instead of the standard file operations that the stem requires.
options.misconception: treats object storage as a file system

explanation: Many functions need one shared set of files with standard file operations. You can access EFS from Lambda by referencing [an EFS file system in your function settings](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-access-from-lambda-function-settings), and the function reaches it [over the local network in a VPC](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-efs-shared-mount-in-vpc). The files stay in EFS between invocations.
takeaway: Lambda functions that share files and keep them between invocations mount Amazon EFS.
twin: If the stem said "each function needs scratch space for one invocation only" instead: the /tmp directory, because /tmp is [temporary and unique to each execution environment](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-tmp-unique-per-environment).

stem: A company runs a Linux application on Amazon EC2 instances in several Availability Zones. The instances share a data set over NFS. The data set grows by an unpredictable amount each week, and old files are deleted at irregular times. The company wants scalable shared storage. The team must never run out of space and does not want to plan, size or grow the storage capacity. Which storage solution meets these requirements?
keywords: grows by an unpredictable amount each week
does not want to plan, size or grow the storage capacity
share a data set over NFS

options.text: Create an Amazon EFS file system, and add an Amazon CloudWatch alarm and a Lambda function that raise the file system size when it is almost full.
options.why: EFS file systems are [elastic, automatically growing and shrinking](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-elastic-grow-shrink), so there is no size to raise, and the alarm and function add work.

options.text: Create an Amazon FSx for OpenZFS file system with SSD storage, and set its storage capacity to the size that the team expects next year.
options.why: With SSD storage you specify a size and [pay for the amount of storage](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-openzfs-two-storage-classes-intelligent-tiering-and-ssd) that you provision, so the team still plans capacity.
options.misconception: treats a file system with a set size as elastic storage

options.text: Attach an Amazon EBS gp3 volume to each instance, and increase the size of each volume with Elastic Volumes when the data grows.
options.why: Block storage is [attached to single Amazon EC2 instances or containers](../facts/efs.md#efs-decision-guide-block-row-single-instance), so the instances do not share one data set, and someone grows each volume.
options.misconception: believes that a volume on each instance gives the instances one shared data set

options.text: Create an Amazon EFS file system with a mount target in each Availability Zone, and mount the file system on every instance.
options.why: EFS grows and shrinks [without provisioning or managing storage capacity](../facts/efs.md#efs-serverless-elastic-no-provisioning), and instances in several zones share it over NFS.

explanation: The team wants no capacity planning and no resizing work. Amazon EFS is [serverless, fully elastic file storage](../facts/efs.md#efs-serverless-elastic-no-provisioning), and a file system is [elastic, automatically growing and shrinking](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-elastic-grow-shrink) as files are added and removed. There is no size to set, so the data set can grow without work.
takeaway: Shared Linux storage with no size to plan or grow: Amazon EFS.
twin: If the stem said "one instance needs a block device for a database" instead: an Amazon EBS volume, because block storage is [attached to single Amazon EC2 instances or containers](../facts/efs.md#efs-decision-guide-block-row-single-instance).

stem: A company is moving an application to Amazon EC2 instances in two Availability Zones. The instances must read and write the same set of files at the same time. The instances run Windows Server, and users reach the files through SMB shares with permissions from the company's Active Directory. The company wants to move the files from its data center to AWS without changing the application. Which storage solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: SMB shares with permissions from the company's Active Directory

options.text: Create an Amazon EFS file system with a mount target in each Availability Zone, and mount the file system on every instance.
options.why: Using EFS with Windows instances [is not supported](../facts/efs.md#efs-windows-ec2-not-supported), so the Windows Server instances cannot use the file system.

options.text: Create an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ file system that is joined to Active Directory, and map its share on every instance.
options.why: It gives [fully managed Microsoft Windows file servers](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-fully-managed-native-windows-file-servers-smb) over SMB, and you [join it to your Active Directory domain](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-joins-active-directory-for-authentication-and-acls) for the permissions.

options.text: Install file server software on a new EC2 instance with a large Amazon EBS volume, and share the files from it with every instance.
options.why: It can work, but the company runs and patches the Windows file server itself, while FSx gives [fully managed Microsoft Windows file servers](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-fully-managed-native-windows-file-servers-smb).

options.text: Create one Amazon EBS io2 volume with Multi-Attach turned on, and attach the volume to every instance in both Availability Zones.
options.why: Multi-Attach attaches one io2 volume to instances [in the same Availability Zone](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-same-az), so the instances in the second zone cannot attach it.

explanation: Windows Server instances that use SMB shares with Active Directory permissions fit FSx for Windows File Server. The domain provides [user authentication and file- and folder-level access control](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-joins-active-directory-for-authentication-and-acls), so the shares keep their permissions. AWS manages the file servers, so the company patches nothing.
takeaway: Windows instances, SMB shares and Active Directory permissions: FSx for Windows File Server.
twin: If the stem said "The instances run Linux and access the files over NFS" instead: Amazon EFS, because it serves EC2 instances [concurrently from multiple NFS clients](../facts/efs.md#efs-concurrent-access-multiple-clients-multiple-azs).
say: Windows, SMB and Active Directory means FSx for Windows File Server, joined to the domain.

stem: A company runs a short-lived high performance computing (HPC) simulation on Amazon EC2 Linux instances for two weeks. The input data is in an Amazon S3 bucket, and the results must be written back to the bucket. The simulation needs a file system with very high throughput. If a file server fails, the job can read the input from Amazon S3 again and repeat the failed step. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: the job can read the input from Amazon S3 again and repeat the failed step

options.text: Create an FSx for Lustre persistent file system linked to the bucket, and turn on daily automatic backups of the file system.
options.why: It works, but its [data is replicated](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-lustre-persistent-replicated-servers-replaced) and backed up for a job that can reread its input from Amazon S3 after a failure.

options.text: Create an FSx for Lustre scratch file system linked to the bucket, and turn on daily automatic backups to protect the results.
options.why: [Backups aren’t supported on scratch file systems](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-faq-lustre-backups-not-on-scratch), so this configuration does not exist.

options.text: Create an Amazon EFS Regional file system with Provisioned throughput, and copy the input data from the bucket before the job starts.
options.why: FSx for Lustre is built for [machine learning, high performance computing (HPC)](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-decision-guide-lustre-speed-workloads), and this option adds a full copy of the input before the job can start.
options.misconception: picks the general-purpose file system for an HPC job on S3 data

options.text: Create an FSx for Lustre scratch file system linked to the bucket, and export the results to the bucket when the job ends.
options.why: Scratch is [cost-optimized storage for short-term, processing-heavy workloads](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-lustre-use-scratch-for-short-term-persistent-for-long-term), and the link lets the job [write file system data back to S3](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-lustre-s3-presents-objects-as-files-and-writes-back).

explanation: The job is short-lived, and it can repeat a failed step from the data in Amazon S3. On a scratch file system the [data is not replicated](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-lustre-scratch-temporary-not-replicated), which this job accepts. The link to the bucket [transparently presents S3 objects as files](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-lustre-s3-presents-objects-as-files-and-writes-back), so the job starts without a full copy.
takeaway: A short HPC job that can rerun from S3: FSx for Lustre scratch, linked to the bucket.
twin: If the stem said "the results stay on the file system for months, and the job is sensitive to downtime" instead: a persistent file system, because it fits workloads [sensitive to disruptions in availability](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-lustre-use-scratch-for-short-term-persistent-for-long-term).

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the MOST cost-effective solution.
I mark the constraints: the job is short-lived, the input is in Amazon S3, the results go back to the bucket, the job needs very high throughput, and it can repeat a failed step.
Before I look at the options, I predict an FSx for Lustre scratch file system linked to the bucket, because scratch is cost-optimized storage for short-term, processing-heavy workloads.

I remove the scratch file system with daily backups, because backups are not supported on scratch file systems. I remove Amazon EFS, because FSx for Lustre is the file system built for HPC, and the EFS option copies the whole input first.

Between the persistent file system and the scratch file system the difference is replication; the stem says the job can read its input from Amazon S3 again, so I do not pay for replicated data and backups.
Check: the scratch file system linked to the bucket meets every constraint, and it writes the results back to the bucket. Time: 90 seconds.

stem: A company runs a Linux application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The instances share a set of files through an Amazon EFS file system. The files are production reports, and the file system must be highly available if one Availability Zone fails. The company plans to create a new file system for these files. Which file system configuration will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: highly available if one Availability Zone fails

options.text: Create an EFS One Zone file system in one Availability Zone, and keep the automatic backups of the new file system turned on.
options.why: One Zone is [not resilient to a complete AZ outage](../facts/efs.md#efs-onezone-not-resilient-to-az-outage), and a backup restores the files later instead of keeping them available.

options.text: Create an EFS Regional file system that stores data across Availability Zones, and create a mount target in each zone.
options.why: A Regional file system gives [continuous availability to the data](../facts/efs.md#efs-regional-multi-az-continuous-availability) when one zone fails, and each zone has its own mount target.

options.text: Create an EFS Regional file system, and configure EFS Replication to a destination file system in a second AWS Region.
options.why: It works, but a Regional file system is designed to [sustain data if an AZ is lost](../facts/efs.md#efs-regional-designed-to-sustain-az-loss), so a replica in a second Region adds cost that the stem does not ask for.

options.text: Create two EFS One Zone file systems in two Availability Zones, and keep them in sync with a scheduled AWS DataSync task.
options.why: A scheduled copy runs behind the source, and someone switches the instances to the other file system after a zone fails.
options.misconception: treats a scheduled copy as high availability

explanation: The stem asks for files that stay available when a zone fails. A Regional file system stores data across [multiple geographically separated Availability Zones](../facts/efs.md#efs-regional-recommended-type), so the instances reach the data through the mount targets in the other zones. One Zone file systems [store data redundantly within a single AZ](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-one-zone-single-az), so a zone outage stops access.
takeaway: Files that stay available through a zone failure: an EFS Regional file system, not One Zone.
twin: If the stem said "The files are development build artifacts that the team can re-create, and a loss of access during an Availability Zone outage is acceptable" instead: One Zone, because it suits [development, build, and staging environments](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-one-zone-use-cases).

stem: A company runs Microsoft SQL Server failover cluster instances on Amazon EC2 instances that run Windows Server in two Availability Zones. The cluster needs shared storage over SMB for the database files. The storage must be highly available across the two Availability Zones and must give the low latency that a database needs. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: highly available across the two Availability Zones

options.text: Create an Amazon EFS Regional file system with mount targets in both Availability Zones, and store the database files on the file system.
options.why: The cluster nodes run Windows Server, and using EFS with Windows instances [is not supported](../facts/efs.md#efs-windows-ec2-not-supported).

options.text: Create an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ file system with SSD storage, and join it to the company's Active Directory domain.
options.why: Multi-AZ uses [a preferred AZ and a standby AZ](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-multi-az-standby-two-azs-sync-replication), and [SSD storage is recommended for SQL Server](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-sql-server-ssd-recommended).

options.text: Create one Amazon EBS io2 volume with Multi-Attach turned on, and attach the volume to the cluster nodes in both Availability Zones.
options.why: Multi-Attach works for instances [in the same Availability Zone](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-same-az), so the node in the second zone cannot attach the volume.

options.text: Create continuously available (CA) file shares on the FSx file system, and store the SQL Server data files and log files on those shares.
options.why: For SQL Server, AWS requires that you [use CA shares on Multi-AZ file systems](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-ca-shares-required-multi-az-for-sql-server).

options.text: Build a Windows file server cluster on two more EC2 instances in the two Availability Zones, and share their EBS volumes over SMB.
options.why: It can work, but the team builds, patches and fails over the file servers itself, while FSx gives [fully managed Microsoft Windows file servers](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-fully-managed-native-windows-file-servers-smb).

explanation: The cluster needs SMB storage that both zones reach. FSx for Windows File Server can be [storage for active data files](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-sql-server-active-data-files-or-share-witness-ssd) of high availability SQL Server. A Multi-AZ file system keeps the shares available by [failing over automatically to the standby AZ](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-multi-az-enhanced-durability-availability-auto-failover).
takeaway: SQL Server clusters across two zones on SMB: FSx for Windows Multi-AZ with SSD and CA shares.
twin: If the stem said "one SQL Server instance in one Availability Zone that uses block storage" instead: an Amazon EBS volume, because block storage is [attached to single Amazon EC2 instances or containers](../facts/efs.md#efs-decision-guide-block-row-single-instance).

stem: A company stores about 100 GiB of application data on an Amazon EFS Regional file system that uses Bursting throughput. The file system has used all of its burst credits, and the application slows down. The application drives a steady-state, predictable throughput close to its peak all day. The company must restore the performance of the application. Which change will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: steady-state, predictable throughput close to its peak all day
used all of its burst credits

options.text: Switch the file system to Elastic throughput, so that throughput scales up and down with the reads and writes of the application.
options.why: Elastic works, but AWS says to use Provisioned throughput when you [know your workload's performance requirements](../facts/efs.md#efs-provisioned-use-when-known-needs-5-percent-or-more), as the company does here.
options.misconception: pays per use for a constant, high throughput

options.text: Switch the file system to Provisioned throughput, and set the provisioned level to the throughput that the application needs at its peak.
options.why: AWS names Provisioned throughput for [predictable and high levels of sustained throughput requirements](../facts/efs.md#efs-pricing-provisioned-throughput-predictable-sustained), and the level is [independent of the file system's size](../facts/efs.md#efs-provisioned-throughput-independent-of-size).

options.text: Keep Bursting throughput, and store extra unused data in the file system to raise the baseline throughput that the file system earns.
options.why: Bursting gives [throughput that scales with the amount of storage](../facts/efs.md#efs-bursting-scales-with-storage-size-recommended-for), so the company pays to store data that nobody reads.

options.text: Create a new file system that uses the Max I/O performance mode, and copy the application data to the new file system.
options.why: Max I/O changes the performance mode, not the throughput mode, and AWS recommends [always using General Purpose performance mode](../facts/efs.md#efs-general-purpose-always-recommended-max-io-higher-latency).

explanation: The load is steady, predictable and close to its peak, so the company knows the throughput that it needs. With Provisioned throughput, [you specify a level of throughput](../facts/efs.md#efs-provisioned-throughput-independent-of-size) that the file system can drive, whatever its size or burst credits. Elastic throughput fits [spiky or unpredictable workloads](../facts/efs.md#efs-elastic-best-for-spiky-low-average-to-peak), which this load is not.
takeaway: Steady, known, high EFS throughput: Provisioned throughput at the level that the application needs.
twin: If the stem said "The throughput is spiky and unpredictable: the application is idle most of the day, then drives short peaks" instead: Elastic throughput, because it fits [spiky or unpredictable workloads](../facts/efs.md#efs-elastic-best-for-spiky-low-average-to-peak).

stem: A company stores 80 TB of engineering files on one Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP volume. Engineers edit about 10% of the files every week, and those files need SSD latency. The other files are infrequently accessed. An administrator created the volume with the AWS CLI and did not set a tiering policy. The company wants to lower the storage cost without slowing down the active files. Which change will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: created the volume with the AWS CLI and did not set a tiering policy

options.text: Change the tiering policy of the volume to All, so that all user data and snapshot data move to capacity pool storage.
options.why: All [marks all user data and snapshot data](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-ontap-tiering-policy-all-marks-everything-cold) as cold, so the files that engineers edit every week leave the SSD tier.
options.misconception: moves active data to the cold tier to save the most money

options.text: Keep the default tiering policy of the volume, because the default policy already moves cold user data to capacity pool storage.
options.why: A volume created with the AWS CLI gets Snapshot Only, which [moves only snapshot data](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-ontap-tiering-policy-snapshot-only-2-days-default-cli), so the cold user files stay on SSD storage.
options.misconception: believes that every new ONTAP volume moves cold user data to capacity pool storage

options.text: Change the tiering policy of the volume to Auto, so that cold user data and snapshots move to capacity pool storage.
options.why: Auto moves cold user data and snapshots after a cooling period that [by default is 31 days](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-ontap-tiering-policy-auto-31-days-default-console), while the active files stay on SSD.

options.text: Change the tiering policy of the volume to None, and increase the SSD storage capacity of the file system for future growth.
options.why: It works, but None [keeps all of your volume’s data](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-ontap-tiering-policy-none-keeps-all-on-ssd) on the SSD tier, so the company keeps paying SSD storage for the cold files.
options.misconception: buys more SSD storage instead of tiering the cold data

explanation: Most of the data is cold, and the active files need SSD latency. With the AWS CLI the default policy is Snapshot Only, which [moves only snapshot data](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-ontap-tiering-policy-snapshot-only-2-days-default-cli). The Auto policy also moves cold user data to the capacity pool tier, so the cold files stop using SSD storage, and the weekly files stay fast.
takeaway: On FSx for ONTAP, mostly cold data with an active part: set the tiering policy to Auto.
twin: If the stem said "all of the files are infrequently accessed archives" instead: the All policy, because it [marks all user data and snapshot data](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-ontap-tiering-policy-all-marks-everything-cold) as cold.

stem: A company keeps application files on an Amazon EFS file system in the us-east-1 Region. The application runs on Amazon EC2 instances in that Region. The company needs cross-Region disaster recovery in us-west-2, with a recovery point objective (RPO) and a recovery time objective (RTO) of minutes. The solution must use ongoing replication. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create an EFS replication configuration for the file system, with a new destination file system in the us-west-2 Region.
options.why: EFS replication copies the file system to the [Region or Availability Zone (AZ) of your choice](../facts/efs.md#efs-replication-destination-faq-region-or-az-of-choice), and [replication is continual](../facts/efs.md#efs-replication-rpo-rto-minutes).

options.text: Point the application in us-west-2 at the replica for writes while replication runs, so that both Regions stay active.
options.why: While replication is enabled, the replica is a [new read-only destination file system](../facts/efs.md#efs-replication-destination-read-only-while-replicating), so the writes in us-west-2 fail.

options.text: Create an AWS Backup plan that backs up the file system every day and copies each recovery point to us-west-2.
options.why: A daily backup leaves the copy in us-west-2 a day behind at worst, which misses an RPO of minutes.
options.misconception: treats daily backup copies as replication with an RPO of minutes

options.text: Run a script on an Amazon EC2 instance that copies changed files to a file system in us-west-2 every minute.
options.why: It can work, but the team runs the instance and the script, while EFS replication works [without having to manage additional infrastructure](../facts/efs.md#efs-replication-destination-faq-region-or-az-of-choice).
options.misconception: builds a custom copy job instead of the built-in replication

options.text: During a disaster, delete the replication configuration so that the replica becomes writeable, and mount the replica in us-west-2.
options.why: To fail over, you delete the replication configuration, and then [the replica becomes writeable](../facts/efs.md#efs-replication-failover-delete-configuration-replica-writeable) for the application in us-west-2.

explanation: EFS replication is designed to provide a recovery point objective (RPO) and a recovery time [objective (RTO) of minutes](../facts/efs.md#efs-replication-rpo-rto-minutes). In a disaster you fail over to the replica [by deleting its replication configuration](../facts/efs.md#efs-replication-failover-delete-configuration-replica-writeable), and the replica then takes the writes.
takeaway: EFS disaster recovery in another Region: EFS replication, then delete the configuration to fail over.
twin: If the stem said "read-only access for users in us-west-2" instead: the replication configuration alone, because applications can [use the replica file system in read-only mode](../facts/efs.md#efs-replication-destination-read-only-while-replicating).
